A.7.1.title: Protected site boundaries
A.7.1.objective: Understand whether physical boundaries protect the information and assets inside the assessed locations.

questions.prompt: Are the boundaries of protected areas clear and matched to where sensitive information and equipment actually sit?
questions.help: Consider offices, storage, shared buildings and provider locations in scope. A floor plan, marked area or practical walkthrough can explain the boundary.
questions.remediation: Align the protected boundary with the sensitive locations and assets.

questions.prompt: Do the physical barriers make unauthorized crossing of that boundary difficult enough for the assessed risks?
questions.help: Explain doors, walls, reception arrangements or equivalent barriers, including shared routes. Choose protection for the actual exposure rather than assuming every site needs fences or guards.
questions.remediation: Strengthen exposed boundary points using proportionate physical safeguards.

questions.prompt: Are damaged or bypassed boundary protections identified and put right?
questions.help: Describe how propped doors, broken locks or changed layouts are noticed and handled. A walkthrough or local reporting arrangement may work; no fixed inspection interval is imposed.
questions.remediation: Resolve degraded protections and keep the boundary aligned with site changes.

A.7.2.title: Controlled site entry
A.7.2.objective: Understand whether physical entry to protected areas follows current authorization and controlled visitor or delivery arrangements.

questions.prompt: Is entry permission limited to people who have a current reason to enter the protected area?
questions.help: Explain approval and the permitted areas for workers and relevant external people. A maintained list, controlled keys or another effective arrangement may be used.
questions.remediation: Limit entry rights to approved people and the areas they need.

questions.prompt: Are physical entry rights removed when the need ends?
questions.help: Consider leavers, role changes and lost keys or credentials. Check the actual removal of access rather than only an update to a staff list.
questions.remediation: Remove obsolete entry rights and address affected credentials.

questions.prompt: Is authorization checked at the routes into protected areas?
questions.help: Consider normal doors and alternate routes, including access from public or shared space. Locks, reception checks or electronic controls may be appropriate; a badge system is not the only solution.
questions.remediation: Close entry routes that bypass the intended authorization check.

questions.prompt: Are visitors kept within the areas and activities they are allowed to access?
questions.help: Explain how a visitor is identified, approved and supervised as needed for the site's exposure. If no visit has occurred, describe the ready procedure rather than inventing a visitor record.
questions.remediation: Establish visitor handling that prevents access beyond the approved purpose.

questions.prompt: Do delivery or collection routes give external people a route into, or alongside, protected areas?
questions.help: Consider goods entrance, couriers and collection areas. This concerns an entry route only. Not relevant here requires a reason and does not exclude this control.

questions.prompt: Are relevant delivery and collection routes controlled to prevent unauthorized access to protected areas?
questions.help: Explain separation, supervised handover, restricted times or equivalent arrangements suitable for the route. A dedicated loading bay is not required.
questions.remediation: Control the relevant handover routes and prevent unintended entry.

A.7.3.title: Protected facilities
A.7.3.objective: Understand whether rooms and facilities receive physical protection suited to the information and activities they contain.

questions.prompt: Have the physical protection needs of the offices, rooms and facilities been identified?
questions.help: Consider sensitive work, stored records, equipment and shared access. Use the actual locations, including facilities operated on your behalf.
questions.remediation: Identify location-specific physical protection needs.

questions.prompt: Do safeguards at those rooms and facilities restrict unauthorized access?
questions.help: Explain doors, windows, storage and internal access arrangements. Existing building controls or equivalent local measures may satisfy the need; a named physical-security product is not required.
questions.remediation: Apply safeguards at the rooms and facilities with identified exposure.

questions.prompt: Does protection continue when the room or facility is unattended?
questions.help: Consider closing procedures and shared premises. Describe actual operation rather than relying on a lock that remains unused.
questions.remediation: Close gaps in protection when relevant facilities are unattended.

questions.prompt: Is sensitive activity inside protected facilities shielded from unintended observation?
questions.help: Consider public corridors, windows or shared work areas. Layout changes, blinds or equivalent measures can address the exposure without mandating a particular building design.
questions.remediation: Reduce unintended visibility into sensitive rooms and work areas.

A.7.4.title: Physical intrusion monitoring
A.7.4.objective: Understand whether monitoring of physical access can identify intrusions and lead to a useful response.

questions.prompt: Does physical intrusion monitoring cover the protected locations and entry routes that need it?
questions.help: Explain the intended coverage and known blind spots. Staff observation, alarms, guards, cameras or a suitable combination may be used; account for privacy obligations.
questions.remediation: Resolve material blind spots in the selected physical monitoring arrangement.

questions.prompt: Is the selected monitoring arrangement operating well enough to detect unauthorized physical access when protection is needed?
questions.help: Consider monitoring while premises are unattended and how failures are noticed. Demonstrate operation through a safe check, exercise or event; buying equipment alone does not establish coverage.
questions.remediation: Restore or improve physical detection where it is unavailable or ineffective.

questions.prompt: Does a detected intrusion reach someone able to investigate and act?
questions.help: Explain the response route, including provider handoffs and out-of-hours coverage where needed. If no intrusion has happened, describe established response readiness.
questions.remediation: Connect physical alerts to a workable investigation and response route.

A.7.5.title: Environmental hazard protection
A.7.5.objective: Understand whether assessed physical and environmental hazards have suitable protective measures.

questions.prompt: Have physical and environmental threats to the assessed locations been considered?
questions.help: Consider fire, water, extreme weather, deliberate damage and other relevant local threats. Climate-related exposure can be considered where relevant; this question does not require a separate climate programme.
questions.remediation: Assess the hazards that could damage or disrupt the actual locations.

questions.prompt: Are safeguards in place for the hazards identified as needing protection?
questions.help: Use measures suited to the local exposure, such as safe siting, detection, suppression or protective building arrangements. No particular protection system is prescribed for every site.
questions.remediation: Implement proportionate safeguards for the identified hazards.

questions.prompt: Are the selected hazard protections kept in working condition?
questions.help: Explain suitable inspection, maintenance or test arrangements for the protection used, including provider-operated measures. Follow applicable safety rules and actual risk needs rather than an invented universal interval.
questions.remediation: Address failed or unverified hazard protections and their upkeep.

A.7.6.title: Secure-area working practices
A.7.6.objective: Understand whether activity inside secure areas follows practical rules that prevent unauthorized exposure or interference.

questions.prompt: Are working rules clear for the activities allowed inside secure areas?
questions.help: Explain what staff and relevant external personnel may do in the area. Rules can sit in existing instructions; a separate policy with a prescribed title is not required.
questions.remediation: Clarify practical rules for work in the protected area.

questions.prompt: Are people working in secure areas kept within their authorized activities?
questions.help: Consider supervision of visitors or contractors where needed and unattended work. A local supervisor or other effective arrangement may be suitable.
questions.remediation: Resolve uncontrolled activity or supervision gaps within secure areas.

questions.prompt: Are recording devices and other information-capture activities restricted according to the area's protection needs?
questions.help: Consider photographs, audio, personal devices or similar capture where relevant. Explain effective restrictions or equivalent protections rather than assuming a universal device ban.
questions.remediation: Apply proportionate restrictions on capture that could expose sensitive work.

A.7.7.title: Clear desks and screens
A.7.7.objective: Understand whether paper, removable media and screens are protected when workspaces are unattended.

questions.prompt: Are expectations for leaving sensitive workspaces clear to the people using them?
questions.help: Include shared desks and remote work where relevant. Existing instructions or briefings can explain how to leave a workspace safely.
questions.remediation: Clarify how people should protect their workspace when leaving it.

questions.prompt: Are sensitive papers and media secured when unattended?
questions.help: Consider storage, shared desks and collection points such as printers. Lockable storage, controlled rooms or another effective approach may be used.
questions.remediation: Secure sensitive papers and media at unattended workspaces.

questions.prompt: Are unattended screens protected against unauthorized viewing or use?
questions.help: Explain manual locking, suitable automatic locking or equivalent access protection. Use settings suited to the work and risk rather than a universal timeout.
questions.remediation: Close gaps in screen locking or equivalent unattended-access protection.

A.7.8.title: Protected equipment placement
A.7.8.objective: Understand whether equipment placement and physical protection reduce avoidable damage and information exposure.

questions.prompt: Is equipment placed to reduce the physical and environmental threats relevant to it?
questions.help: Consider public reach, water, heat and accidental damage at the actual location. Safe layout or protective housing can be appropriate alternatives.
questions.remediation: Move or protect equipment exposed to avoidable physical hazards.

questions.prompt: Does the placement or protection of equipment limit unauthorized physical access and observation?
questions.help: Consider screens, ports and equipment in shared areas. Layout, barriers or controlled access may provide suitable protection without requiring one equipment enclosure.
questions.remediation: Reduce unauthorized reach or viewing created by equipment placement.

questions.prompt: Do the actual equipment locations still match the selected protection measures?
questions.help: Check moved devices, temporary installations and changed surroundings. An observed walkthrough can support this answer; no required inspection document title is imposed.
questions.remediation: Address placement changes that undermine the equipment's safeguards.

A.7.9.title: Off-site asset safeguards
A.7.9.objective: Understand whether assets remain protected while transported, used or stored away from normal premises.

questions.prompt: Is off-site use or custody of assets authorized and accountable?
questions.help: Consider laptops, records, media and other relevant assets, including provider custody. A checkout record, assigned custodian or equivalent arrangement may be used.
questions.remediation: Clarify permission and custody for assets taken or held off-site.

questions.prompt: Are assets protected against the loss, damage and unauthorized access relevant to their off-site use?
questions.help: Consider transit, temporary storage, home working and public places. Locks, careful handling, protected transport or suitable technical safeguards may be used according to risk.
questions.remediation: Apply proportionate safeguards to exposed off-site assets.

questions.prompt: Is there a workable way to report and contain loss or compromise of an off-site asset?
questions.help: Explain how custodians raise an issue and how affected information is protected. If no loss has occurred, describe readiness; a mandatory remote-wipe product is not assumed.
questions.remediation: Establish prompt reporting and suitable containment for off-site loss.

A.7.10.title: Media lifecycle safeguards
A.7.10.objective: Understand whether storage media is protected throughout acquisition, use, movement and retirement.

questions.prompt: Are handling rules for storage media matched to the sensitivity of the information it can hold?
questions.help: Consider removable and fixed media and how custody is assigned. Existing classification and handling instructions can provide the rules; a separate media policy title is not required.
questions.remediation: Define appropriate handling for the media and information in use.

questions.prompt: Is media protected against unauthorized access or damage during use and storage?
questions.help: Explain controlled access and storage appropriate to the media. Physical safeguards, access restrictions, encryption or suitable combinations may be used.
questions.remediation: Close gaps in protection of media during use or storage.

questions.prompt: Is media movement controlled so information remains protected and custody remains clear?
questions.help: Consider internal handover and external transport actually used. Accountable handover or a reliable provider arrangement can work; a particular courier or form is not required.
questions.remediation: Protect media during transfer and resolve unclear custody.

questions.prompt: Is stored information made unrecoverable to unauthorized recipients before media is reused or disposed of?
questions.help: Choose a method suitable for the medium and its sensitivity. Confirm the result rather than assuming a disposal receipt proves sanitization; do not remove information subject to a valid retention hold.
questions.remediation: Apply and verify suitable information removal before media leaves authorized use.

A.7.11.title: Utility resilience
A.7.11.objective: Understand whether supporting utilities can sustain the protection and operation needs of information processing.

questions.prompt: Have the supporting utilities needed by the assessed equipment been identified?
questions.help: Consider power, cooling, communication or other utilities actually relied on. Include shared building and provider dependencies where relevant.
questions.remediation: Identify utility dependencies and their effects on information processing.

questions.prompt: Do the utility arrangements protect information processing against the disruptions that need to be addressed?
questions.help: Compare protection with service needs. Safe shutdown, alternate supply, provider resilience or another suitable approach may be used; no universal generator or runtime is specified.
questions.remediation: Address utility disruptions that exceed the accepted service or information risks.

questions.prompt: Are the selected utility protections maintained and checked for their intended operating needs?
questions.help: Use safe checks, service records or provider assurance appropriate to the arrangement. Explain unresolved faults; the interval follows the actual design and obligations.
questions.remediation: Restore failed utility protections and establish suitable readiness checks.

A.7.12.title: Protected cabling
A.7.12.objective: Understand whether power and communication cabling is protected from the risks affecting the services and information it carries.

questions.prompt: Have important cable routes and their physical exposure been identified?
questions.help: Consider power and data routes, shared buildings and provider responsibility. A diagram or knowledgeable walkthrough can establish the relevant routes.
questions.remediation: Identify exposed cable routes needed for the assessed services.

questions.prompt: Is cabling protected against the damage or interference relevant to those routes?
questions.help: Consider routing, separation, conduit or equivalent measures appropriate to the environment. Do not assume every cable requires a particular shield or installation method.
questions.remediation: Reduce avoidable cable damage or interference along the relevant routes.

questions.prompt: Is access to sensitive cables and connection points controlled against interception or tampering?
questions.help: Consider exposed connections, shared wiring areas and access for servicing. Physical restriction, protected routes or equivalent measures may address the risk.
questions.remediation: Restrict exposed connection points and sensitive cable routes.

A.7.13.title: Equipment servicing
A.7.13.objective: Understand whether maintenance sustains equipment operation while controlling technician access and information exposure.

questions.prompt: Is equipment maintained in a way that supports its required availability and integrity?
questions.help: Explain servicing based on equipment needs and relevant manufacturer advice. Include provider-maintained equipment where used without imposing a blanket calendar interval.
questions.remediation: Address equipment whose required maintenance is missing or ineffective.

questions.prompt: Is maintenance access limited to authorized people and the work they need to perform?
questions.help: Consider on-site and remote access and supervision where needed. Approval, controlled access or equivalent arrangements may work.
questions.remediation: Restrict maintenance access and prevent unapproved servicing activity.

questions.prompt: Is information protected against exposure during maintenance?
questions.help: Consider diagnostic access, technician tools and the data on equipment. Access limits, sanitization, supervised work or suitable equivalents may be used.
questions.remediation: Close information-exposure gaps during equipment service.

questions.prompt: Can maintenance involve taking equipment or storage components outside the organization's controlled locations?
questions.help: Include return-to-vendor service and external repair. This concerns the off-site service route only; Not relevant here requires a reason and leaves the core maintenance questions active.

questions.prompt: Is information protected before equipment is released for relevant off-site servicing?
questions.help: Use sanitization, protected custody or another justified method suitable to the information and repair needs. A service supplier's name alone does not establish protection.
questions.remediation: Establish protected release and custody for off-site maintenance.

questions.prompt: Are affected security safeguards checked before serviced equipment returns to normal use?
questions.help: Consider altered settings, replacement parts and restored access restrictions. A relevant functional check or service verification can support the answer.
questions.remediation: Verify affected safeguards after servicing and resolve failures.

A.7.14.title: Equipment retirement and reuse
A.7.14.objective: Understand whether equipment can be reused or retired without releasing sensitive information or retained software rights.

questions.prompt: Is equipment checked for stored sensitive information and licensed software before reuse or retirement?
questions.help: Include embedded storage in printers or appliances where relevant. The check can use an asset review or equivalent process; do not infer that a device is empty from its appearance.
questions.remediation: Identify stored information and licensed software that need treatment before release.

questions.prompt: Is sensitive information removed using a method suited to the equipment and its next use?
questions.help: Consider sanitization or destruction appropriate to the medium and sensitivity. Ordinary file deletion is not proof of removal; preserve records that still have valid retention duties.
questions.remediation: Apply suitable sanitization or destruction before equipment release.

questions.prompt: Are licensed software and related access entitlements handled appropriately before equipment is transferred or reused?
questions.help: Follow the actual licensing and access terms; reassignment or removal may be appropriate. This does not require uninstalling all software regardless of its permitted next use.
questions.remediation: Resolve software or entitlement exposure incompatible with the intended transfer.

questions.prompt: Is the outcome of information removal checked before equipment is released?
questions.help: Explain a verification appropriate to the sanitization method and media. A provider certificate can contribute but must relate to the device and result; no prescribed certificate title is required.
questions.remediation: Confirm information removal and prevent release when the result is uncertain.

A.8.1.title: Endpoint safeguards
A.8.1.objective: Understand whether user endpoints receive safeguards suitable to their information, use and exposure.

questions.prompt: Do the selected safeguards cover the user endpoints that handle information in scope?
questions.help: Consider laptops, phones, remote devices and personally owned devices where permitted. Management reports or another reliable reconciliation can show coverage without requiring a particular device-management platform.
questions.remediation: Identify and address endpoints outside the intended protection coverage.

questions.prompt: Are safeguards on those endpoints appropriate to the information and activities they support?
questions.help: Consider local data, unauthorized use and exposure during remote work. Access controls, protected storage, suitable configuration or equivalent measures may be used according to risk.
questions.remediation: Apply appropriate safeguards to the assessed endpoint uses.

questions.prompt: Are failed or missing endpoint protections detected and addressed?
questions.help: Consider disabled controls, unsupported devices and exceptions. Explain the operational response rather than treating enrollment or purchase of software as proof of protection.
questions.remediation: Resolve failed protections and unmanaged exceptions across active endpoints.

A.8.2.title: Privileged permissions
A.8.2.objective: Understand whether elevated permissions are justified, restricted and controlled throughout their use.

questions.prompt: Is each privileged entitlement justified by the work that needs elevated access?
questions.help: Include human and service accounts where relevant. Evaluate the privilege actually granted; do not assume every administrator needs permanent access.
questions.remediation: Reduce privileges that exceed the justified operational need.

questions.prompt: Is privileged access authorized before it is granted?
questions.help: Explain an accountable authorization route suitable to the organization. A request record or another traceable decision can work without requiring a dedicated privileged-access product.
questions.remediation: Establish approval for granting elevated permissions.

questions.prompt: Is elevated access used under safeguards that limit unnecessary or unaccountable privileged activity?
questions.help: Consider separate administrative use, restricted duration, controlled service identities or suitable equivalents. Select safeguards for the actual work rather than assuming one universal access model.
questions.remediation: Constrain unnecessary or unaccountable elevated activity.

questions.prompt: Are privileged permissions reduced or removed when their justification changes?
questions.help: Consider role changes, departures, temporary tasks and emergency access. Use actual need and organizational review arrangements rather than an invented fixed cadence.
questions.remediation: Remove or reduce elevated permissions no longer justified.

A.8.3.title: Restricted information access
A.8.3.objective: Understand whether access to information follows the established access rules across relevant paths.

questions.prompt: Are the permitted users and actions clear for the information being protected?
questions.help: Consider information sensitivity and roles, including service or provider access. Existing access rules can be used without inventing a new permission model.
questions.remediation: Clarify who may perform which actions on the protected information.

questions.prompt: Are those restrictions enforced where information is actually accessed?
questions.help: Consider applications, files, APIs, queries and exports that exist in the environment. A hidden button or an intended role description alone does not establish enforced access.
questions.remediation: Enforce intended restrictions at the actual access paths.

questions.prompt: Do alternate access routes preserve the same information restrictions?
questions.help: Consider indirect access, shared links and provider routes where used. Use representative permission checks; this does not mandate one testing tool.
questions.remediation: Close alternate routes that expose information beyond authorized access.

questions.prompt: Are information permissions kept aligned with changes in need?
questions.help: Explain how access changes and obsolete permissions are handled. Existing access administration can provide this without a separate review platform.
questions.remediation: Resolve permissions that no longer match authorized need.

A.8.4.title: Source-code access
A.8.4.objective: Understand whether source code, development tools and software libraries have controlled read and change access.

questions.prompt: Does access control cover source code and the development tools and software libraries used with it?
questions.help: Consider repositories, build assets and supporting development services actually used, including external providers. Protect the relevant assets rather than only one branch or project.
questions.remediation: Bring relevant development assets within the intended access controls.

questions.prompt: Is the ability to read source code and related development assets limited to authorized need?
questions.help: Consider read-only contributors, exported copies and external parties. Repository permissions or suitable equivalent controls may be used.
questions.remediation: Restrict unnecessary read access to code and development assets.

questions.prompt: Is the ability to modify source code and related development assets limited to approved contributors?
questions.help: Consider write permissions, build changes and protected delivery paths. Existing review and authorization arrangements may work without prescribing a particular repository vendor.
questions.remediation: Restrict changes to approved contributors and controlled paths.

questions.prompt: Is development-asset access removed or changed when a person's or provider's need changes?
questions.help: Consider departures, changed projects and ended engagements. A permission review can demonstrate this; no fixed interval is invented.
questions.remediation: Remove stale or excessive development-asset permissions.

A.8.5.title: Authentication safeguards
A.8.5.objective: Understand whether authentication gives appropriate assurance of identity across the actual access and recovery paths.

questions.prompt: Is the authentication approach suited to the sensitivity and risk of the access it permits?
questions.help: Consider normal, administrative and service access. Different suitable methods can be used; selecting this answer does not mean a named authentication product or every possible factor is required.
questions.remediation: Select authentication appropriate to the protected access.

questions.prompt: Is the intended authentication enforced across the relevant access paths?
questions.help: Consider legacy, remote and provider-managed paths where used. Inspect actual enforcement rather than a setting that applies to only some users.
questions.remediation: Close paths that bypass the intended authentication.

questions.prompt: Are authentication attempts handled so unauthorized users cannot readily defeat the process?
questions.help: Consider the relevant risks from repeated attempts, disclosed credentials and authentication error messages. Suitable built-in protections or equivalent measures can be used.
questions.remediation: Address weaknesses in how authentication attempts are handled.

questions.prompt: Do recovery or alternate authentication arrangements preserve suitable identity assurance?
questions.help: Consider resets, fallback and support-assisted recovery where available. If none is offered, explain how the normal method remains recoverable or usable; this is not a whole-control applicability decision.
questions.remediation: Resolve recovery paths that undermine the intended identity assurance.

A.8.6.title: Capacity planning
A.8.6.objective: Understand whether resource capacity is measured and adjusted to meet current and expected demand.

questions.prompt: Is use of the resources that could constrain the service measured or otherwise reliably understood?
questions.help: Consider processing, storage, connections or people where relevant to the capacity decision. Measurements, provider reports or suitable observations may be used.
questions.remediation: Establish useful visibility of the resources that constrain service delivery.

questions.prompt: Are expected capacity needs considered before demand exceeds available resources?
questions.help: Consider growth, peak activity and planned changes. A practical forecast or reviewed estimate can work without requiring a capacity-planning product.
questions.remediation: Assess expected demand and the resources needed to support it.

questions.prompt: Are capacity limits addressed in time to protect the required service?
questions.help: Explain scaling, reducing avoidable load, provider action or other suitable responses. No universal utilization threshold or review interval is imposed.
questions.remediation: Address constraints before they impair the required service.

A.8.7.title: Malware defences
A.8.7.objective: Understand whether malware protections cover relevant exposure and support detection, recovery and user awareness.

questions.prompt: Are malware-prevention measures in place for the platforms and entry routes needing them?
questions.help: Consider downloads, messages, removable media and software delivery where relevant. Filtering, execution restrictions, platform protections or suitable equivalents may be used.
questions.remediation: Close material gaps in prevention of malicious software.

questions.prompt: Can the organization detect malicious software in the assessed environment?
questions.help: Explain the detection coverage and how missing or failed protections are identified. Installed licenses alone do not establish functioning coverage.
questions.remediation: Address ineffective detection and failed or missing protections.

questions.prompt: Is there a working response to contain malware and recover affected operation?
questions.help: Consider isolation, removal and recovery appropriate to the systems. If no event has occurred, describe established readiness or a safe exercise.
questions.remediation: Establish or improve containment and recovery from malware.

questions.prompt: Do relevant users know the precautions and reporting steps that reduce malware exposure?
questions.help: Use briefings, instructions or suitable training connected to the actual threats. No prescribed course, vendor or annual interval is assumed.
questions.remediation: Clarify practical malware precautions and reporting for relevant users.

A.8.8.title: Vulnerability handling
A.8.8.objective: Understand whether technical weaknesses are identified, evaluated and treated according to actual exposure.

questions.prompt: Is information about technical vulnerabilities obtained for the technology actually in use?
questions.help: Consider operating systems, applications, dependencies and provider services. Supplier notices, appropriate scanning or other reliable sources may be combined without mandating one scanner.
questions.remediation: Establish relevant vulnerability information for the technology population.

questions.prompt: Are identified vulnerabilities evaluated for the exposure and consequences relevant to your environment?
questions.help: Consider whether the affected component is present, how it is reachable and what it protects. A generic severity score alone may not explain the local priority.
questions.remediation: Assess local exposure and prioritize treatment accordingly.

questions.prompt: Are suitable actions taken for vulnerabilities that need treatment?
questions.help: Consider patches, configuration changes, isolation or justified compensating safeguards. Deferrals need an accountable risk decision; no universal patch deadline is invented.
questions.remediation: Carry out suitable treatment and resolve unjustified deferrals.

questions.prompt: Is the result checked before a vulnerability is treated as resolved?
questions.help: Use a relevant recheck, version confirmation or equivalent verification. A closed ticket alone does not establish that the affected exposure changed.
questions.remediation: Verify that treatment addressed the vulnerability or residual exposure.

A.8.9.title: Secure configuration
A.8.9.objective: Understand whether security configurations are established, put into use and kept aligned with approved decisions.

questions.prompt: Are intended security configurations defined for the systems and services in scope?
questions.help: Include hardware, software, networks and relevant cloud services. A documented baseline, approved configuration or equivalent record can express the intended settings.
questions.remediation: Define suitable security settings for the assessed technology.

questions.prompt: Are the intended configurations applied to the relevant technology?
questions.help: Compare actual settings with approved decisions, including provider responsibilities. A template that is not deployed does not establish implementation.
questions.remediation: Apply the intended settings and resolve unmanaged configurations.

questions.prompt: Are departures from approved configurations detected and addressed?
questions.help: Use configuration checks, change review or another suitable approach. Explain accepted deviations and corrective action rather than treating every variation as automatically forbidden.
questions.remediation: Identify and resolve unexplained departures from the intended configuration.

questions.prompt: Are approved configuration decisions updated when relevant needs or technology change?
questions.help: Consider new systems, changed exposure and approved exceptions. Use actual change triggers and chosen review arrangements rather than a mandatory numerical interval.
questions.remediation: Update configuration decisions that no longer match current protection needs.

A.8.10.title: Information deletion
A.8.10.objective: Understand whether information is safely removed when no longer needed under the applicable retention decisions.

questions.prompt: Is it clear when information is no longer needed and can be deleted?
questions.help: Use the applicable business, contractual and legal retention decisions, including valid holds. This interview does not determine a legal retention period or require immediate deletion despite a hold.
questions.remediation: Clarify deletion eligibility and preserve information still subject to a valid need or hold.

questions.prompt: Do deletion arrangements account for the relevant systems and managed copies of that information?
questions.help: Consider replicas, exports, service providers and backups under the selected retention design. Deferred backup expiry can be appropriate when controlled; do not invent universal immediate erasure of every historical copy.
questions.remediation: Address unmanaged copies or provider-held information omitted from deletion decisions.

questions.prompt: Is eligible information actually deleted using an appropriate method?
questions.help: Consider the storage technology, sensitivity and possible recovery. Application deletion, controlled expiry, sanitization or a suitable equivalent can be used according to the intended outcome.
questions.remediation: Implement appropriate removal of information eligible for deletion.

questions.prompt: Are failed or incomplete deletions identified and followed up?
questions.help: Use an execution check, service confirmation or a representative result review. A retention configuration alone does not establish that deletion occurred.
questions.remediation: Detect and address information left behind by failed deletion.

A.8.11.title: Data masking
A.8.11.objective: Understand whether masking reduces unnecessary exposure while preserving the appropriate restrictions on original information.

questions.prompt: Are the data and uses needing reduced exposure identified?
questions.help: Consider reports, support views, analytics or testing actually used. Start from information sensitivity and access needs rather than applying cosmetic masking to every field.
questions.remediation: Identify where exposing full values exceeds the user's or process's need.

questions.prompt: Does the selected masking or equivalent transformation prevent recipients from receiving unnecessary sensitive values?
questions.help: Consider redaction, pseudonymization, anonymization or other suitable techniques. The technique must fit the use and actual privacy obligations; masking is not automatically anonymization.
questions.remediation: Correct transformations that still expose unnecessary sensitive values.

questions.prompt: Have reconstruction or re-identification risks been considered for the transformed outputs?
questions.help: Consider combinations of fields, linked datasets and reversal methods relevant to the technique. A representative output check can be useful without imposing one de-identification test on every use.
questions.remediation: Address practical ways recipients could reconstruct protected values.

questions.prompt: Is access to original values or reversal information restricted to authorized need?
questions.help: Consider originals, lookup tables and keys where the technique uses them. Controlling the output alone does not protect an openly accessible source.
questions.remediation: Restrict original or reversal information that defeats the selected masking.

A.8.12.title: Data-loss prevention
A.8.12.objective: Understand whether measures address inappropriate disclosure or movement of sensitive information through the actual routes in use.

questions.prompt: Are the sensitive information and routes at risk of inappropriate disclosure understood?
questions.help: Consider transfer, storage and processing routes actually used, including endpoints and services. Existing data-flow knowledge can suffice without requiring a dedicated discovery product.
questions.remediation: Identify sensitive information routes omitted from the protection design.

questions.prompt: Are suitable measures applied to those routes to prevent or detect inappropriate disclosure?
questions.help: Consider access limits, transfer restrictions, content inspection or appropriate equivalent measures. A product marketed as DLP is not mandatory, and privacy obligations still apply.
questions.remediation: Close material gaps in protection of sensitive information routes.

questions.prompt: Do the selected measures work for representative leakage scenarios?
questions.help: Use a safe test, observed operating result or relevant provider assurance. Do not transmit real sensitive information merely to demonstrate a control.
questions.remediation: Verify and correct ineffective measures on the intended routes.

questions.prompt: Is detected or reported information leakage assessed and acted on?
questions.help: Explain investigation and containment appropriate to the exposure. If no event has occurred, describe readiness rather than assuming no alerts proves protection.
questions.remediation: Connect leakage detections or reports to suitable investigation and action.

A.8.13.title: Recoverable backups
A.8.13.objective: Understand whether backups cover the recovery need, remain protected and can restore usable information.

questions.prompt: Do backup arrangements cover the information, software and system state needed for recovery?
questions.help: Consider the recovery needs set by the organization and the provider responsibilities where applicable. Select backup scope and timing from those needs rather than a universal daily rule.
questions.remediation: Resolve omissions in the backup coverage needed for recovery.

questions.prompt: Are backup copies protected against unauthorized access, alteration and loss?
questions.help: Consider separation from the same incident affecting the primary system. Access limits, encryption, isolated copies or appropriate equivalents may be used according to risk.
questions.remediation: Address exposures that could compromise the backup copies.

questions.prompt: Are backup failures identified and corrected?
questions.help: Consider actual job outcomes or provider confirmation and what happens to missed copies. A configured schedule alone does not show successful operation.
questions.remediation: Detect and resolve failed or incomplete backup operation.

questions.prompt: Are backups tested by restoring usable information or systems for the intended recovery need?
questions.help: Compare the restored result with actual business recovery needs. Use suitable restoration tests and chosen timing; a successful copy job is a different result.
questions.remediation: Establish or improve restoration checks that demonstrate usable recovery.

A.8.14.title: Processing redundancy
A.8.14.objective: Understand whether processing redundancy can meet the defined availability need rather than only duplicating components.

questions.prompt: Are the availability needs that redundancy is intended to support clear?
questions.help: Use actual service needs and accepted disruption, including provider commitments. This does not impose a universal uptime percentage or multi-region design.
questions.remediation: Clarify the availability outcome the redundant arrangement must support.

questions.prompt: Does the redundant arrangement address failure of the components needed for that availability outcome?
questions.help: Consider power, network, storage and other shared dependencies. Alternate systems or services may work; two components sharing a critical failure path may not.
questions.remediation: Address shared dependencies or uncovered failures that defeat redundancy.

questions.prompt: Can the service continue or recover through the selected redundancy when the primary path fails?
questions.help: Use an appropriate failover exercise, operational example or provider assurance. Avoid disrupting live service for the interview; test design and timing follow actual needs.
questions.remediation: Verify and correct the ability to use redundancy during failure.

A.8.15.title: Security event logs
A.8.15.objective: Understand whether event logging provides useful, protected records that can support investigation.

questions.prompt: Are the events needed to investigate security-relevant activity recorded across the assessed systems?
questions.help: Consider significant user, administrative, failure and exception events appropriate to the environment. Define useful coverage without logging every possible activity or sensitive payload.
questions.remediation: Address important events or systems missing from logging.

questions.prompt: Do event records contain enough context to interpret the activity?
questions.help: Consider attribution, time, action and result appropriate to the event. Do not collect credentials, tokens or unnecessary personal data to make a log appear complete.
questions.remediation: Improve missing event context while minimizing sensitive data.

questions.prompt: Are logs protected against unauthorized access, tampering and loss?
questions.help: Consider access by the people whose activity is logged and the effect of a compromised system. Separate storage, limited permissions or suitable equivalent protection may be used.
questions.remediation: Protect logs from unauthorized changes, exposure or loss.

questions.prompt: Are logs retained and retrievable for the organization's investigation and applicable retention needs?
questions.help: Use actual needs and obligations; no universal retention period or named logging platform is prescribed.
questions.remediation: Resolve retention or retrieval gaps that prevent useful investigation.

questions.prompt: Are relevant event records analyzed so significant issues can be recognized?
questions.help: Explain review or automated analysis appropriate to the events and risks. The logging control's record analysis is distinct from the wider activity-monitoring interview.
questions.remediation: Establish useful analysis of significant recorded events.

A.8.16.title: Activity monitoring
A.8.16.objective: Understand whether activity monitoring identifies anomalous behavior and connects it to investigation.

questions.prompt: Does monitoring cover the networks, systems and applications relevant to detecting adverse activity?
questions.help: Include provider telemetry and handoffs where used. Define the actual coverage rather than assuming one centralized monitoring product is required.
questions.remediation: Close material gaps in the monitored environment.

questions.prompt: Is monitored activity evaluated for unusual behavior that could indicate a security incident?
questions.help: Use suitable baselines, rules, analysis or human review connected to relevant threats. Not every deviation is an incident; an accountable assessment is needed.
questions.remediation: Improve detection of adverse activity relevant to the environment.

questions.prompt: Do relevant monitoring signals reach a working triage and investigation process?
questions.help: Explain responsibilities and response appropriate to the signal. If no significant signal has occurred, describe established readiness rather than inventing an investigation.
questions.remediation: Connect monitoring signals to appropriate triage and investigation.

questions.prompt: Are missing telemetry and ineffective monitoring identified and addressed?
questions.help: Consider disconnected sources, disabled rules and provider coverage changes. Suitable tests or coverage checks may be used without imposing a fixed schedule.
questions.remediation: Restore missing telemetry and correct ineffective monitoring coverage.

A.8.17.title: Aligned system clocks
A.8.17.objective: Understand whether relevant system clocks use aligned time references that support reliable event interpretation.

questions.prompt: Are suitable time references selected for the systems whose records need to be interpreted together?
questions.help: Consider provider systems and distributed environments where relevant. An approved internal or external reference can be used; a particular public time service is not mandatory.
questions.remediation: Select consistent time references for the relevant systems.

questions.prompt: Are the relevant system clocks synchronized with those time references?
questions.help: Consider actual configuration and observed alignment. Different time-zone displays do not by themselves mean clocks are misaligned; evaluate the timestamps used for correlation.
questions.remediation: Align relevant system clocks with the selected time references.

questions.prompt: Are synchronization failures or material clock drift noticed and addressed?
questions.help: Use health checks, alerts or another appropriate observation. The acceptable accuracy follows the records' use and actual obligations; no universal tolerance or interval is imposed.
questions.remediation: Detect and resolve clock drift that undermines event interpretation.

A.8.18.title: Privileged utility use
A.8.18.objective: Understand whether utilities capable of bypassing normal safeguards are restricted and used under accountable control.

questions.prompt: Are the utilities that can override normal system or application safeguards identified?
questions.help: Consider administrative consoles, diagnostic tools and powerful scripts actually available. An existing inventory or knowledgeable review can establish the scope.
questions.remediation: Identify utilities whose capabilities bypass ordinary safeguards.

questions.prompt: Is access to those utilities limited to people and tasks with an authorized need?
questions.help: Consider installation, execution and supporting privileges. Restricted permissions or other suitable controls may work without mandating a dedicated utility-management product.
questions.remediation: Restrict access to safeguard-bypassing utilities.

questions.prompt: Is use of a privileged utility authorized for its intended purpose?
questions.help: Explain the allowed tasks and how exceptional use is approved. Existing administrative procedures can provide this without requiring an approval ticket for every harmless command.
questions.remediation: Clarify and enforce the authorized purposes of powerful utility use.

questions.prompt: Can significant privileged-utility activity be traced and examined?
questions.help: Use logs, supervised work or equivalent records appropriate to the risk. The utility's availability or an administrator's job title alone does not establish accountable use.
questions.remediation: Establish useful accountability for significant safeguard-bypassing activity.

A.8.19.title: Software installation controls
A.8.19.objective: Understand whether operational software is installed through controlled and secure procedures.

questions.prompt: Are permitted software installations on operational systems defined?
questions.help: Include user, administrator and provider deployment routes. Existing software and change rules may be used without requiring a separate installation policy title.
questions.remediation: Clarify the software and installation routes permitted in operation.

questions.prompt: Do actual installation permissions and deployment paths prevent unauthorized software from entering operation?
questions.help: Consider privileged users as well as ordinary users. Permissions, managed deployment or suitable equivalent restrictions can be used.
questions.remediation: Close installation paths that bypass the approved permissions.

questions.prompt: Are approved installations carried out with appropriate safeguards for the operational system?
questions.help: Consider trusted software sources, relevant compatibility checks and recovery options. Use the existing deployment procedure suited to the system rather than requiring one package manager.
questions.remediation: Strengthen installation procedures that expose the operational system to avoidable risk.

questions.prompt: Are failed or unauthorized installation outcomes identified and addressed?
questions.help: Use relevant deployment results or software checks. Explain how exceptions are resolved; a successful installer exit alone may not show healthy operation.
questions.remediation: Resolve installation failures and unauthorized software in operation.

A.8.20.title: Network protection
A.8.20.objective: Understand whether networks and network devices protect the information and services carried through them.

questions.prompt: Are the relevant network connections and exposed services understood?
questions.help: Consider internal, external, remote and provider connections actually used. Current diagrams, configuration or another reliable view may show the exposure.
questions.remediation: Identify network paths and services omitted from the protection design.

questions.prompt: Are safeguards applied to the network paths according to their information and service risks?
questions.help: Consider traffic restrictions, secure protocols and boundary protection suited to the topology. Equivalent protections are acceptable; no firewall vendor is prescribed.
questions.remediation: Address inadequately protected network paths and services.

questions.prompt: Is administration of network devices controlled against unauthorized or unsafe changes?
questions.help: Consider device access and configuration, including provider responsibilities. Existing access and change procedures can supply suitable control.
questions.remediation: Restrict and control administrative changes to network devices.

questions.prompt: Do the active network protections still reflect current connections and authorized exceptions?
questions.help: Review representative rules or operation after relevant changes. A current configuration check can work without requiring one monitoring product or fixed schedule.
questions.remediation: Correct stale rules or exceptions that leave unintended exposure.

A.8.21.title: Network-service safeguards
A.8.21.objective: Understand whether network services have clear security needs, agreed delivery arrangements and oversight of actual safeguards.

questions.prompt: Are security mechanisms needed from the network services identified?
questions.help: Consider connectivity, remote access, wireless and other services actually used. Requirements can be expressed in service settings or existing agreements without a prescribed document title.
questions.remediation: Define the safeguards needed from the relevant network services.

questions.prompt: Are required service levels clear for the network services relied on?
questions.help: Use actual availability, capacity or response needs relevant to the service. Do not invent universal uptime or provider response targets.
questions.remediation: Clarify the service levels the network arrangement needs to support.

questions.prompt: Are the security needs reflected in the arrangements governing how the network service is delivered?
questions.help: Include internal services and provider services. An internal operating agreement or suitable contract can express the arrangement; outsourcing does not remove organizational oversight.
questions.remediation: Address delivery arrangements that omit the required safeguards.

questions.prompt: Is there a working way to establish that network-service safeguards are delivered as expected?
questions.help: Use configuration checks, service reviews, testing or relevant provider assurance. A contract or provider name alone does not establish actual delivery.
questions.remediation: Obtain suitable assurance and follow up gaps in the delivered safeguards.

A.8.22.title: Network segmentation
A.8.22.objective: Understand whether separation between network groups limits unauthorized communication and incident spread.

questions.prompt: Are the network groups needing separation identified according to their trust and protection needs?
questions.help: Consider users, services, administration and devices appropriate to the environment. Zones, separate networks or suitable logical boundaries may be used.
questions.remediation: Define network groups and boundaries that address the relevant exposure.

questions.prompt: Is communication between those groups restricted to the flows they are meant to allow?
questions.help: Consider actual traffic rules rather than the diagram alone. VLANs, filtering, separate networks or equivalent enforcement must achieve the intended restriction.
questions.remediation: Close unintended traffic paths across network groups.

questions.prompt: Do representative connection checks show that the intended boundaries work?
questions.help: Consider whether a low-trust or compromised segment can reach protected services. Use safe checks or observed traffic; do not launch disruptive attacks to answer the interview.
questions.remediation: Verify and correct segment boundaries that permit unintended access.

A.8.23.title: Web-content controls
A.8.23.objective: Understand whether access to external web content is managed to reduce exposure to malicious or inappropriate content.

questions.prompt: Are the web-content risks and intended access restrictions clear?
questions.help: Consider relevant users, devices and business access needs. Existing acceptable-use rules can support the decision without inventing a universal blocked-category list.
questions.remediation: Clarify web risks and proportionate access restrictions.

questions.prompt: Are suitable web-content protections applied across the intended access routes?
questions.help: Consider office, remote, mobile and provider-managed routes where used. Filtering, protected browsing or an effective equivalent can be appropriate without a prescribed vendor.
questions.remediation: Close routes that bypass the intended web-content protection.

questions.prompt: Are allowed exceptions controlled so they do not undermine the intended protection?
questions.help: Explain legitimate access, authorization and removal of obsolete exceptions. A bounded exception can be appropriate; unrestricted bypass is a different outcome.
questions.remediation: Resolve unbounded or obsolete web-content exceptions.

questions.prompt: Are failed or ineffective web-content restrictions recognized and corrected?
questions.help: Use representative access checks, operating results or provider assurance. Purchasing a filtering service alone does not establish enforcement.
questions.remediation: Correct ineffective restrictions on the intended users and routes.

A.8.24.title: Cryptographic safeguards
A.8.24.objective: Understand whether cryptographic use and key management support the information protection needs.

questions.prompt: Are the purposes and rules for using cryptography clear for the information being protected?
questions.help: Consider storage, transfer and other relevant uses and actual legal or contractual constraints. Existing policy and design decisions may supply the rules.
questions.remediation: Clarify where and how cryptography is intended to protect information.

questions.prompt: Is suitable cryptography actually applied where those rules require it?
questions.help: Consider real configurations and coverage, including provider-managed services. Use established mechanisms appropriate to risk; no single algorithm or product is universally prescribed here.
questions.remediation: Resolve missing or unsuitable cryptographic protection at the intended uses.

questions.prompt: Is access to cryptographic keys restricted to the people and processes that need it?
questions.help: Consider key storage, backup and administrative access. Managed services, controlled files or other suitable custody arrangements can be used. Never include key material in an interview answer.
questions.remediation: Restrict key access and protect key material from disclosure.

questions.prompt: Are keys managed through creation, use, replacement and retirement according to their protection needs?
questions.help: Include recovery where needed and handling of suspected compromise. Choose timing and methods from actual needs and obligations rather than a universal rotation interval.
questions.remediation: Resolve missing lifecycle or compromise handling for cryptographic keys.

questions.prompt: Which cryptographic arrangement is used? (Optional)
questions.help: A service or role description may help the conversation. Unknown tool or owner names do not decide implementation status. Do not supply keys, secrets or certificates containing private material.

A.8.25.title: Secure development lifecycle
A.8.25.objective: Understand whether security rules influence software and system development throughout their lifecycle.

questions.prompt: Are security rules defined for the development and maintenance work in scope?
questions.help: Include internal and external work and the lifecycle stages actually used. An existing delivery process can carry the rules without requiring a separate methodology or policy title.
questions.remediation: Define security activities appropriate to the actual development lifecycle.

questions.prompt: Are those security activities carried out through the relevant development stages?
questions.help: Consider requirements, design, build, testing and maintenance as used in the delivery approach. A lightweight process can work; checking security only at the final release may leave earlier decisions unexamined.
questions.remediation: Apply the selected security activities at the stages where they affect decisions.

questions.prompt: Do security results influence decisions about delivery and subsequent maintenance?
questions.help: Explain how material issues are corrected or subject to an accountable decision before acceptance. Existing release controls can provide this without inventing a universal gate or zero-defect rule.
questions.remediation: Connect security activity results to delivery and maintenance decisions.

A.8.26.title: Application security needs
A.8.26.objective: Understand whether application security needs are identified and accepted before development or acquisition decisions are finalized.

questions.prompt: Are application security requirements identified from the intended use, information and relevant obligations?
questions.help: Include applications acquired as services as well as those built internally. Consider users, sensitive information and misuse appropriate to the application without inventing legal applicability.
questions.remediation: Identify security needs omitted from the application's intended use.

questions.prompt: Are the relevant security requirements agreed with the people deciding or delivering the application?
questions.help: Consider business, technical and provider responsibilities actually involved. A requirements record or existing procurement process may work without requiring a named committee.
questions.remediation: Resolve disagreement or missing agreement on application security requirements.

questions.prompt: Are the security requirements clear enough to guide acceptance of the application?
questions.help: Consider how important access, protection and resilience needs will be evaluated. Tests, reviews or appropriate provider assurance may be used; a requirement merely labeled 'secure' is not necessarily testable.
questions.remediation: Make important security requirements evaluable at application acceptance.

questions.prompt: Are application security requirements reconsidered when the intended use or material risks change?
questions.help: Use relevant design or acquisition changes. No universal review interval is imposed, and this does not create a new requirements-management system.
questions.remediation: Update requirements that no longer match the application and its exposure.

A.8.27.title: Secure architecture principles
A.8.27.objective: Understand whether security architecture and engineering principles guide system design and consequential changes.

questions.prompt: Are security architecture and engineering principles established for the systems in scope?
questions.help: Consider trust boundaries, least privilege, failure handling and other principles relevant to the system. Existing engineering standards can express them without mandating one architecture framework.
questions.remediation: Clarify principles suitable to the system's protection needs.

questions.prompt: Do consequential design decisions apply those principles to the system's actual threats and boundaries?
questions.help: Use a relevant design decision or review. Equivalent architectures can meet the purpose; a diagram or principle list alone does not establish application.
questions.remediation: Address design decisions that disregard the relevant security principles.

questions.prompt: Are significant system changes examined for their effect on the security design?
questions.help: Consider interfaces, dependencies and approved trade-offs. The depth of review follows the change's risk; do not demand a complete redesign for every minor change.
questions.remediation: Review material changes and resolve newly exposed security boundaries.

A.8.28.title: Secure coding practices
A.8.28.objective: Understand whether coding practices prevent avoidable security defects and lead to correction of unsafe code.

questions.prompt: Are secure coding practices defined for the languages and technologies actually used?
questions.help: Consider input handling, access control and other relevant defect classes. Existing language guidance or team standards may work; no named standard or tool is required for every team.
questions.remediation: Define coding practices addressing the actual technologies and defect risks.

questions.prompt: Do developers apply those practices in the code they produce or change?
questions.help: Use a representative change to discuss how unsafe patterns are avoided. Include external contributors where used without treating a written standard as proof of application.
questions.remediation: Address unsafe patterns that conflict with the selected coding practices.

questions.prompt: Is code examined for security defects using methods appropriate to its risk?
questions.help: Peer review, relevant analysis or suitable combinations can work. No single scanning product is mandatory, and generated code still needs appropriate examination.
questions.remediation: Improve code examination where relevant defects are missed.

questions.prompt: Are material coding defects corrected or resolved through an accountable risk decision?
questions.help: Follow the finding through the actual correction and relevant recheck. A completed review or ignored tool warning alone does not establish correction.
questions.remediation: Resolve material coding defects and verify the relevant changes.

A.8.29.title: Security testing before acceptance
A.8.29.objective: Understand whether security testing during development and acceptance evaluates the relevant risks and affects acceptance decisions.

questions.prompt: Are security tests defined to address the relevant requirements and risks?
questions.help: Consider development and acceptance stages, negative cases and important boundaries. Appropriate manual, automated or provider testing may be used without requiring one technique for every system.
questions.remediation: Address security risks or requirements omitted from the test scope.

questions.prompt: Are the selected security tests actually performed at the relevant development and acceptance stages?
questions.help: Use actual results for a representative delivery. A plan or product license alone does not demonstrate test execution.
questions.remediation: Carry out the selected tests at the stages where results can affect delivery.

questions.prompt: Are significant issues found by security tests followed through to a suitable outcome?
questions.help: Consider correction and relevant retesting or an accountable residual-risk decision. This does not require every finding to have the same severity or treatment.
questions.remediation: Resolve significant test issues and establish the result of treatment.

questions.prompt: Does acceptance of the system take security test results and remaining risks into account?
questions.help: Explain who can accept the delivery under the actual rules and what supports that decision. A green build is not necessarily acceptance of security results.
questions.remediation: Connect acceptance to the relevant security results and remaining risks.

A.8.30.title: Outsourced development oversight
A.8.30.objective: Understand whether development performed by external parties remains directed, monitored and accepted under the organization's security needs.

questions.prompt: Are security expectations for outsourced development agreed with the external party?
questions.help: Consider the work and deliverables actually commissioned, including changes and supporting development assets. Existing agreements can carry the expectations without a prescribed contract template.
questions.remediation: Agree security expectations omitted from the external development arrangement.

questions.prompt: Is outsourced development monitored enough to identify departures from those expectations?
questions.help: Use progress review, development evidence or suitable assurance matched to the delivery risk. Outsourcing does not itself demonstrate secure development.
questions.remediation: Establish useful visibility and follow-up over external development work.

questions.prompt: Are external deliverables evaluated against the agreed security needs before acceptance?
questions.help: Use review, testing or other suitable assurance for the deliverable. The supplier's reputation or certificate alone may not establish the delivered result.
questions.remediation: Obtain suitable security assurance before accepting external deliverables.

questions.prompt: Are development security gaps or material changes raised with the supplier and followed through?
questions.help: Explain correction, clarification or accountable residual-risk decisions as appropriate. If none has occurred, describe the ready escalation route.
questions.remediation: Resolve supplier development gaps and changes that affect agreed protection.

A.8.31.title: Separated development and production
A.8.31.objective: Understand whether development and testing are separated from production sufficiently to protect live information and services.

questions.prompt: Are development, testing and production separated according to the risks of cross-environment activity?
questions.help: Physical or logical separation may be suitable. Consider shared services and provider environments; a separate cloud account for every stage is not universally required.
questions.remediation: Establish boundaries suited to the development and production exposure.

questions.prompt: Are permissions controlled so development or test activity cannot make unapproved production changes?
questions.help: Consider administrators, deployment identities and shared credentials where relevant. Separation must work in actual permissions, not only environment names.
questions.remediation: Restrict uncontrolled production access from development or testing.

questions.prompt: Do changes move into production through an authorized path that preserves the intended separation?
questions.help: Use the actual deployment procedure, including provider handoffs. An existing reviewed release process can work without prescribing a particular pipeline.
questions.remediation: Close promotion paths that bypass the intended environment controls.

questions.prompt: Is movement of production information into development or testing controlled against unnecessary exposure?
questions.help: Consider copies, access and sanitization where used. Synthetic data or protected live-derived data can be appropriate alternatives; this is not permission to export customer data for the interview.
questions.remediation: Control production-data movement that undermines environment separation.

A.8.32.title: Controlled changes
A.8.32.objective: Understand whether changes affecting information processing receive proportionate impact decisions, authorization and implementation checks.

questions.prompt: Are relevant information-security effects assessed before changes are made?
questions.help: Consider services, configurations and system changes in scope. Use an existing change review appropriate to the risk rather than imposing the same paperwork on every change.
questions.remediation: Assess security effects omitted from change decisions.

questions.prompt: Are changes authorized by an appropriate decision route before normal implementation?
questions.help: Consider routine and significant changes under the actual rules. A delegated standard-change route may be suitable; a named change board is not required.
questions.remediation: Establish suitable authorization for changes affecting information processing.

questions.prompt: Are changes implemented with safeguards proportionate to the risk of failure?
questions.help: Consider relevant testing, recovery options and communication needed for the actual change. A rollback plan, retained version or suitable equivalent can protect operation without mandating a universal template.
questions.remediation: Address changes lacking suitable failure or recovery safeguards.

questions.prompt: Are affected services and safeguards checked after implementation?
questions.help: Compare the result with the intended change and follow up failures. A completed deployment command alone does not establish the intended operational result.
questions.remediation: Verify changed operation and resolve unintended effects.

questions.prompt: Can urgent changes affecting information processing need to proceed sooner than normal change lead times allow?
questions.help: Consider realistic incidents or service-restoration needs. Assess the urgency in the operating environment, not whether an urgent procedure already exists. Not relevant here requires a reason and leaves normal change control active.

questions.prompt: Does the urgent route preserve appropriate authorization and subsequent review?
questions.help: Describe the actual route and follow-up, including provider work where relevant. If no urgent change has occurred, explain readiness without inventing a completed record.
questions.remediation: Close urgent-change gaps in accountable authorization or subsequent review.

A.8.33.title: Protected test information
A.8.33.objective: Understand whether test information is selected and handled without unnecessarily exposing sensitive source information.

questions.prompt: Is test information chosen to meet the test need while limiting unnecessary sensitive information?
questions.help: Consider synthetic or suitably transformed data as alternatives. Live-derived data may need justification and protection; realistic testing does not automatically require full production records.
questions.remediation: Reduce unnecessary sensitive information in test data.

questions.prompt: Is test information protected according to its sensitivity and permitted use?
questions.help: Consider access, storage and transfer in internal or provider test environments. Masking or equivalent transformation can help but does not replace suitable access protection.
questions.remediation: Address exposure of test information beyond its permitted use.

questions.prompt: Can tests use information copied or derived from live sensitive records?
questions.help: Consider retained identifiers and linkable transformed data, not only full records. This concerns the live-derived subpart; Not relevant here requires a reason and leaves the core test-information questions active.

questions.prompt: Is sensitive live-derived information authorized and appropriately minimized before test use?
questions.help: Explain the actual need, approval and protective transformation or equivalent safeguards. Do not copy live data as part of answering this interview.
questions.remediation: Resolve unjustified or unprotected live-derived information in testing.

questions.prompt: Is test information retained or removed according to its approved purpose and retention needs?
questions.help: Consider leftover datasets, provider copies and repeated test runs. Controlled retention can be appropriate; no universal deletion deadline is imposed.
questions.remediation: Address test information kept or exposed beyond its permitted need.

A.8.34.title: Safe audit testing
A.8.34.objective: Understand whether audit testing of operational systems is agreed and controlled to protect services and information.

questions.prompt: Are the audit test scope and access agreed with the appropriate operational decision makers before testing?
questions.help: Include provider-operated systems where relevant. Agreement can use existing test planning and authorization; this does not authorize testing merely because an auditor requests it.
questions.remediation: Agree the scope and access before operational audit testing.

questions.prompt: Is audit-test access limited to what the agreed test needs?
questions.help: Consider read-only access where suitable, accounts, tools and data handling. More intrusive access needs an appropriate reason and safeguards rather than an assumed right to administrator access.
questions.remediation: Restrict audit-test access and information exposure to the agreed need.

questions.prompt: Are safeguards in place for test activity that could disrupt services or affect information?
questions.help: Consider timing, recovery and stop conditions appropriate to the test. A non-disruptive alternative can be suitable; no test should be launched merely to answer this interview.
questions.remediation: Establish safeguards for disruptive or information-affecting test activity.

questions.prompt: Can relevant operational people monitor the test and stop it if its agreed limits are exceeded?
questions.help: Explain coordination or supervision suitable to the test and exposure. If no test has occurred, describe the ready arrangement.
questions.remediation: Clarify operational monitoring and the ability to stop unsafe test activity.

questions.prompt: Is temporary test access or test-created information handled appropriately when testing ends?
questions.help: Consider removing temporary privileges and protecting or removing copies according to the agreed need. Existing access and evidence procedures may supply the closure.
questions.remediation: Resolve retained test access or information outside the agreed post-test need.
